label: Convex Independent Subsets
notes: Chapter three asks a single sharp question across printed pages twenty-nine to forty: how many planar points force a convex polygon of a chosen size. We frame convex independent sets, preview the Erdos-Szekeres guarantee, and motivate the cups-and-caps engine and Horton sets that close the empty-polygon variant.

label: Convex Position
notes: A finite set is convex independent when none of its points lies in the convex hull of the others, so every point is a genuine vertex of the polygon they span. This vertex condition is the exact object Erdos and Szekeres count, and it survives any affine map of the plane.

label: The Erdos-Szekeres Problem
notes: For each target size we seek the threshold count above which every general-position set must hide a convex polygon with that many vertices. Generality rules out three collinear points so orientations stay decisive. The chapter proves this threshold is finite and bounds it from both directions.

label: Cups and Caps
notes: The proof replaces hard convex polygons with two ordered chains. A cup is a sequence whose slopes increase, bending upward, while a cap has decreasing slopes bending downward. Sorting points by x-coordinate turns the geometric question into monotone subsequence bookkeeping that recursion can attack cleanly.

label: The Cup-Cap Lemma
notes: The central lemma counts points needed to force a k-cup or an l-cap. Its bound is one plus the binomial of k plus l minus four choosing k minus two. The recursion splits points by whether they end a long cup or begin a long cap, mirroring Pascal's identity exactly.

label: Recursion Engine
notes: Each point gets a label: the longest cup ending there. If no label reaches k we read a long cap from points sharing a label, because between equal-label neighbors the slope must drop. This pigeonhole between cup growth and cap formation drives the binomial induction to its conclusion.

label: The Convex Polygon Bound
notes: A convex n-gon contains both a cup and a cap, so forcing one chain of size n forces convex position. Combining the lemma gives an upper threshold of one plus the binomial of two n minus four choosing n minus two points, roughly four to the n, guaranteeing n convex-independent points.

label: Lower Bound Construction
notes: To show the threshold is genuinely exponential we build large sets with no convex n-gon. Stacking carefully scaled cup-shaped clusters, each tiny relative to the previous, prevents any long cup or cap from spanning groups. This yields sets of size two to the n minus two avoiding convex n-gons.

label: Empty Convex Polygons
notes: A sharper demand asks for an empty convex polygon, one whose interior holds no other point of the set. Five points always give an empty quadrilateral and large sets force empty pentagons, but Horton discovered that empty heptagons can be avoided forever by special configurations.

label: Horton Sets
notes: Horton sets are built recursively by splitting into a high part and a low part, each a scaled Horton set, interleaved in x so neither can be enclosed emptily by the other. The key property is that no seven points of a Horton set form an empty convex heptagon, defeating naive expectations.

label: Why Horton Sets Work
notes: The defeating mechanism is that any cup in the lower half is shielded by a point of the upper half sitting inside it, and symmetrically for caps. This interleaving destroys every candidate empty heptagon, so empty-polygon Ramsey behaviour diverges sharply from the ordinary Erdos-Szekeres guarantee.

label: Synthesis
notes: We close by aligning the three layers: the convex-independence definition, the cup-cap recursion bounding the threshold between exponential walls, and Horton sets exposing the empty-polygon gap. Each invariant, hull size, cup length, and emptiness, is a checkable quantity the notebook turns into executable diagrams and counts.
